Rehabiah
ree-ha-BYE-ah
n. (proper, son of Eliezer the son of Moses; Hebrew, the LORD has enlarged)
Hebrew Rechabyah, from rachab, to be wide or enlarged, and Yah — Jehovah has enlarged. He is the only son of Eliezer, who was the second son of Moses, and the note attached to him is a quiet marvel.

Biblical Definition

The Chronicler is recording the Levitical houses and pauses over Moses' own descendants: “And the sons of Eliezer were, Rehabiah the chief. And Eliezer had none other sons; but the sons of Rehabiah were very many” (1 Chronicles 23:17) — the margin reads were highly multiplied. One son, and from that one son a multitude. He appears again in the courses: “Concerning Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, the first was Isshiah” (1 Chronicles 24:21), and among the keepers of the treasures: “And his brethren by Eliezer; Rehabiah his son, and Jeshaiah his son, and Joram his son, and Zichri his son, and Shelomith his son” (1 Chronicles 26:25). Eliezer was named by Moses because The God of my father, said he, was mine help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh. His grandson bears a name meaning God has enlarged, and the text says the family was highly multiplied.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the only son of Eliezer the son of Moses, whose own sons were very many.

expand to see more

ENLARGE, v.t. To make greater in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits, breadth or size; to increase.

MULTIPLY, v.i. To increase in number; to extend; to grow or become more numerous by propagation.

POSTERITY, n. Descendants; children, children's children, and so on indefinitely.

TREASURY, n. A place or building in which stores of wealth are reposited; the place where the public revenues are deposited.

OBSCURITY, n. A state of being unknown to fame; a humble condition; privacy.

Modern Corruption

Significance is measured by what a man leaves that bears his own name; Moses' sons appear only in a Levitical list, and the line runs on through one grandson whom nobody remembers.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The striking thing about Rehabiah is whose grandson he is. Moses had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, and neither succeeded him in anything. The leadership went to Joshua, the priesthood to Aaron's line, and Moses' own descendants appear in Chronicles as ordinary Levites over the treasures. There is no dynasty. Whatever else the greatest prophet of the Old Testament left behind, it was not a family office, and the Holy Ghost records the fact without a syllable of complaint.

What was given instead is in the verse itself. Eliezer had none other sons — a single line, easily broken — but the sons of Rehabiah were very many, and the Hebrew margin says highly multiplied. Eliezer's own name means my God is an help, given because God had delivered Moses from Pharaoh's sword. Rehabiah's means God has enlarged. From a narrow place God made room. A household reduced to one son is not a household God has finished with, and the record of Moses' line is the proof.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Rechabyah (H7345), Jehovah has enlarged; rachab (H7337), to be wide; Eliyezer (H461), my God is help; rabah (H7235), to multiply.

Hebrew Rechabyah (H7345) — Rehabiah; Jehovah has enlarged.

Hebrew rachab (H7337) — to be or grow wide, to make room; thou hast enlarged me in distress.

Hebrew Eliyezer (H461) — Eliezer, my God is help; his father, the son of Moses.

Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to multiply; the sons of Rehabiah were highly multiplied.

Hebrew Gereshom (H1648) — Gershom, a stranger there; Moses' elder son.
